newsitem.title: UK: Iraq seeks spot oil sales to hit cash target -trade.
newsitem.headline: Iraq seeks spot oil sales to hit cash target -trade.

text.p: Iraq is seeking to sell crude oil on a spot basis to make up for a shortfall in revenue from an oil-for-food plan caused by lower world prices and underperformance by Russian customers, oil traders said on Wednesday.

"Some central European refiners are being offered spot deals," said a trader at a European oil company which lifts Iraqi crude under the terms of the United Nations deal implemented on December 10 last year.

Traders said one refinery in central Europe had already agreed to take a million-barrel cargo from Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organization (SOMO), which was now seeking approval for the sale from the U.N.

Earlier, Western diplomats in New York said a report filed last week to the Iraq sanctions committee at the U.N. put the total value of the first three month's worth of contracts at about $800 million.
Under the terms of the deal, Iraq is permitted to sell $1 billion worth of crude from December 10 to March 9, 1997, and then another $1 billion for the next 90 days.
For the first 90 days of the plan, the U.N. is expected to allow SOMO to make up any shortfall by selling additional oil on the spot market, rather than agreeing new term contracts, diplomats said.
"I don't think (the overseers) would add another contract or change the existing contracts, it would be a one-off cargo to be sold on the spot market," said a diplomat.

Regular SOMO customers said the shortfall was the result of a sharp decline in world oil prices, down almost 14 percent since the beginning of January, and the failure of a number of Russian companies to lift contracted volumes.
"For the time being I'm bound to believe values are falling short of expectations. Some Russian traders do not seem to be performing very well," said one.
Yuri Agababov, deputy director of Zarubezhneft which is co-ordinating Russian purchases of Iraqi oil, said last week Russian companies had lifted five million barrels of oil by February 7.
The companies are contracted to lift 12.5 million barrels by March 9, or 140,000 barrels per day (bpd) over the whole three month period.
To achieve the target, the Russian companies would have to lift 250,000 bpd for the balance of February and the first 10 days of March, a task described as extremely difficult by traders.
"There are no takers for the oil. Even the other contract holders are struggling to swallow it," said one.

Other SOMO customers, including some which had their volumes cut back when prices were high, said they had not been offered extra barrels for the first 90-day period and were expecting to rollover contracts for the second.

The lower-than-expected sales to Russian companies were attributed to shipping delays, problems attaining letters of credit and a relatively short nomination period for Basrah Light loadings which made sales into Far Eastern markets particularly tricky.
"I'm not surprised by the (Russian) underperformance but it's not entirely their fault," said another SOMO customer.
"If you receive allocations for Basrah Light in a six-week time horizon the market has already been covered by then and the barrels are immediately distressed," he added.
